title: Narrative Failure: Russia and the West have a Storytelling Problem
content:
Audiences respond to stories that drive toward an achievable climax. In the big movie of this summer, Odysseus faces endless challenges on his way home to Ithaca, but we know his goal is to reunite with Penelope and Telemachus and that he is handy with a bow. The story proceeds in an arc to his ultimate triumph.

Both Russia and the West have tried to promote a logical arc for the end of the Ukraine war, but their narratives have lacked goals and means. Both sides have failed to define exactly what they want, or to convince the world they have the ability to achieve it.

After Russia’s full-scale invasion, Western nations promised to give Ukraine “whatever it takes” without ever defining “it.” President Joe Biden’s administration never fixed a goal of entirely rolling back the invasion, nor did its European allies.

Three months after the invasion, Biden even implied Russia might keep some of its early territorial gains. He said the US would help Ukraine fight “further” aggression so it would “be in the strongest possible position at the negotiating table.”

title: Russian Fertilizer: Nourishing the Roots of War
content:
Russian fertilizer makers have largely escaped sanctions, despite their importance for revenues, the provision of war materiel, and strategic leverage. There are no sanctions on products entering the US, and the European Union (EU) only imposed curbs in mid-2025.

As a result, the Russian fertilizer industry has enjoyed a booming export market in the EU and US since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. At the same time, the Kremlin’s manipulation of European gas supply has devastated EU manufacturers, enhancing opportunities for exporters.

And the proprietors of these businesses, such as Ultrachem’s Dmitry Mazepin and Eurochem’s Andrey Melnichenko, are not neutral businessmen. They are close to the Russian leadership, have been personally sanctioned by the EU, and provide vital explosives for the war.

Russia’s fertilizer industry has become a major economic and military security threat, which Western allies need to tackle.

title: AI Safety – Little Hope for a US-China Deal
content:
Concerns over AI safety are growing, fueled by a series of autonomous agent breakouts and fears that humanity is on the verge of losing control to superintelligent AI swarms. 

After Dario Amodei, CEO of AI leader Anthropic, warned about safety risks, US lawmakers have urged new rules to govern AI systems. Amodei also warned that Chinese dominance could present national security risks, provoking Chinese state media to denounce a “Cold War playbook.” But President Donald ⁠Trump has brushed aside ​calls to slow AI development, saying that “very negative forces” exaggerated concerns. Expect any agreement to be narrowly scoped. 

CEPA fellows see little progress emerging from the upcoming US-China summit in Washington.

James Lewis, Distinguished Fellow

title: Ukraine’s War Widows Fight for Compensation
content:
Ulyana was living at her parents’ home in Ternopil, western Ukraine, when she was told in 2023 that Vlad, her husband of 17 years and a soldier, had died while at a military base near the frontline in eastern Donbas. He was reported to have killed himself.

“Vlad was the most important person in my life,” Ulyana said as she sat at her kitchen table in a two-bedroom apartment in Kyiv. “We lived in harmony.”

Ukraine pays out compensation to war widows and families of fallen soldiers provided certain criteria are met. But in cases where a soldier’s death has been declared suicide, which is classified as a non-combat loss, there is no entitlement to financial support. After Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, Kyiv announced a one-time payment of 15m hryvnias ($340,000) would be offered to families of soldiers killed defending their country on the frontlines. In 2024, the government introduced a second option, which allowed families to claim 2.27m hryvnias, and is typically issued when a soldier dies while on duty, but not at the front.

title: Russia’s Rigged Elections Still Serve a Purpose
content:
The outcome of Russia’s parliamentary elections is predetermined. Yet the Kremlin cares about much more than the figures announced once the ballots are (mis)counted.

Vladimir Putin’s regime can of course falsify almost any result. Independent election monitoring has been largely destroyed, voting has been extended over three days, and electronic ballots are difficult to verify. But an entirely fictional election would cease to perform its most important function. It would tell the Kremlin nothing about the discipline of its officials, the resilience of regional elites, or the state’s ability to mobilize the population.

Russian elections are therefore more than a falsified vote count. They are a nationwide examination of the Putin system. Citizens play a secondary role. The real examinees are governors, bureaucrats, directors of state institutions, and party functionaries.

From September 18 to 20, Russians elect a new State Duma. At the same time, more than 2,200 regional and municipal elections will take place across the country, distributing approximately 20,700 elected offices and legislative seats.
snippet: The outcome of Russia’s parliamentary elections is predetermined. Yet the Kremlin cares about much more than the figures announced once the ballots are (mis)counted.
creator: Sara George

title: Russia’s Election Campaign Puts Governors on the Hook
content:
In the upcoming Russian parliamentary elections from September 18-20, governors will be the top candidate in 45 of the ruling United Russia party’s 57 regional rosters (80%).

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin, who is also considered the governor of the Russian capital, ranks second on the five-candidate federal party roster. Adding other governors running in second place brings the total number of such officials featured at the top of United Russia’s regional and federal rosters to 55. Since 2016, the number of governors heading the party’s rosters has risen sharply: from 19 in that year, to 49 in 2021 and now 55.

This growing reliance is telling. Regional leaders are not merely electoral “coattails” or “locomotives”; they also bear personal responsibility for results in their regions. Voting for United Russia can thus increasingly be seen as a referendum on governors’ approval, shifting accountability for the party’s performance onto their shoulders, and potentially becoming a major pain in their necks. For the party, it’s a useful corrective since it both keeps political elites in step and devolves any electoral uncertainty onto other officials.
snippet: In the upcoming Russian parliamentary elections from September 18-20, governors will be the top candidate in 45 of the ruling United Russia party’s 57 regional rosters (80%).

title: The Big Day Looms for Putin’s Election Fixers
content:
Sergei Kiriyenko became head of the Kremlin’s political bloc after the 2016 State Duma elections. His predecessor, Vyacheslav Volodin, lost his position partly because turnout in those elections fell below 50%, a show of popular apathy too notable to ignore.

Volodin had not wanted to overheat the system. But he worked hard to construct a network of sham public organizations around Putin, each offering unconditional support for the president and his policies. The All-Russia People’s Front was the clearest example.

Under Volodin’s model, a dependent or loyal electorate was expected to turn out on election day. This ensured predictability while also providing a measure of legitimacy. Protest-minded citizens, meanwhile, were expected to stay away from the polls and then draw the obvious conclusion: the authorities had won thanks to the votes of the loyal electorate.

title: Kremlin Vote-Fakers Crush the Liberals
content:
With Russia’s parliamentary elections now imminent, the registration and subsequent hurried removal of the liberal Yabloko’s federal list from the State Duma ballot stand out as the campaign’s most consequential event — both for democratic opposition inside and outside of the country and the Kremlin itself.

The crackdown on the only party openly calling for peace began months before the election, targeting its most prominent figures, and has continued throughout the campaign, which ends with voting from September 18-20. A recent poll by a small, independent research group with access to voters inside Russia suggests Yabloko could have won 20-25% of the vote had it remained on the ballot, challenging the Communist Party (KPRF) for second place behind United Russia.

The authorities have long had ample scope to “adjust” the ruling party’s result by transferring votes between tallies. In 2024, manipulation inflated Putin’s total by 22–25 million votes in the 2024 presidential vote, adding roughly a third to his actual vote count.

title: How to Defeat Russia’s Shadow War
content:
Europe’s response to Russia’s increasingly ferocious attacks on Ukraine and a widening shadow war campaign against European NATO has been familiar: strategic restraint.

That strategy is increasingly outdated. Something new is needed.

Hybrid warfare operates in the space between strategic necessity and military constraint. Both Putin and his entourage are faced with a stalling front line, an unfolding fiscal crisis, and Ukrainian strikes reaching ever further into Russian soil that, in autocratic regime logic, demand an aggressive response, not the negotiating table. Putin must escalate, driven by the realities of regime survival, whether Europe shows restraint or not.

Jonathan Powell, the UK’s national security adviser, who helped negotiate the Good Friday Agreement in Northern Ireland nearly three decades ago, argued on September 13 that the Kremlin’s escalating reaction to Western pressure was “a sign of success” and that Europe should not “take its foot off the gas”.

While the shadow campaign against Europe does not prove Russia is buckling, it does reveal that it is willing to up the ante.
snippet: Europe’s response to Russia’s increasingly ferocious attacks on Ukraine and a widening shadow war campaign against European NATO has been familiar: strategic restraint.
creator: Sara George

title: Everyday Products, Big Risks: China’s Connected Tech Danger
content:
Chinese ZPMC cranes supplied to American ports contained cellular modems that could bypass firewalls, gather information, and disrupt cargo handling. Chinese Yutong buses sold to Oslo came with connected battery and power controls. The Norwegian city’s public transport authority, Ruter, warned that, in theory, the buses “can be stopped or rendered inoperable by the manufacturer.”

Chinese connected vehicles carry cameras, microphones, and location sensors that gather data. Chinese-supplied apps, such as Hikvision’s Hik-Connect, send phone and SIM card identifiers to Chinese servers.

The West long has identified Chinese-supplied telecoms as a danger. It must now wake up and confront the danger of a vast array of Chinese products, ranging from cranes to cameras. Allies need to avoid instituting counterproductive sovereignty requirements. They should build a shared response that limits exposure by private purchase of Chinese consumer goods.
